As the Minister will know, last evening on the CBC national news it was revealed that the Minister for International Trade made extensive use of the Government JetStars during 1981. On 60 per cent of those trips, the Minister, his family, and relatives, rode for free. I would ask the Minister of Transport what the Liberal policy is with respect to free rides for family members on Government JetStars.

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION
subsubtopic: USE OF GOVERNMENT PLANES BY MINISTER OF STATE (INTERNATIONAL TRADE)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Department of Transport planes are made available to members of the Cabinet who travel on Government business. The Minister's department is charged on the basis of the plane operational cost. In other words, the number of people on board the plane does not affect the cost.
I was also on TV yesterday trying to explain that, because of the heavy load on members of Cabinet, which everybody will recognize, travelling affords Cabinet Ministers one of the few opportunities they have to be with their wives and children. I argued this case, and I was promptly chastised by my own wife for not practising what I was preaching.
I have said all of this to indicate that Members of Cabinet use these planes on the honour system. They use them when travelling on Government business, and I tried to explain that having one passenger, or two or three, on board the plane does not make a real difference to what is being charged to the country.

subtopic: AVAILABILITY OF COMMERCIAL FLIGHTS

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AVAILABILITY OF COMMERCIAL FLIGHTS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I direct my supplementary question to the Minister of Transport. What effort is made by Transport Canada to check the availability of regular commercial flights, such as those from Ottawa to Calgary? If the Minister were to take a regular commercial flight, it would save the Government some $1,150 per hour. What effort is made by the Government to check the availability of commercial flights before the free rides take over?

subtopic: AVAILABILITY OF COMMERCIAL FLIGHTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I repeat that the Ministers operate on an honour
Oral Questions
system, and I do not ask every Minister on each occasion if they could have used some other facility of a commercial nature. The guidelines are available for everybody to read. By way of illustration, the guidelines say:
-in the following circumstances:
(a) when a flight is being made to a point where there is no commercial air
service; where no space is available ... where ... substantial savings of
essential time can be made by using departmental aircraft-
Time is a very important consideration. Using myself as an example, very often in the last year and a half I have travelled west on Crow business and, because of the Government airplane, I have had the opportunity to do in one day or half a day what I would not have been able to do in three days using commercial airplanes. This illustrates the phrase "savings of essential time".
I believe that the population as a whole does recognize this. They generally request Cabinet Ministers to be present for many kinds of occasions, for personal negotiations as well as social events, and consequently using the Government airplane is the only way that we can fulfil those requests.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AVAILABILITY OF COMMERCIAL FLIGHTS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we are not very impressed with the Minister's use of the phrase "honour system", because the Government abandoned the honour system a long time ago.

subtopic: COST OF FLIGHT FROM OTTAWA TO CALGARY

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: COST OF FLIGHT FROM OTTAWA TO CALGARY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister specifically about what transpired on April 16, 1981, when the Minister of International Trade flew from Ottawa to Calgary with his wife and three children, even though regular commercial service was available. That trip cost the taxpayers of Canada $10,000. How much advance notice was Transport Canada given of the Minister's requirement for a JetStar for his family on that occasion?

subtopic: COST OF FLIGHT FROM OTTAWA TO CALGARY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, to be able to answer that question fairly, I would have to know about all of the circumstances, and I do not. But I do know that I went to Calgary at about the same time, but I also went to Edmonton and to Regina at the same time. It all depends on the circumstances, and I referred to savings of essential time as one of the criteria that would be helpful to consider when making a judgment on any decision to use a JetStar. Be that as it may, I do not answer for each of the Ministers singly. Each one of them has to justify the flight of a Minister to the public, in general, and follow the guidelines. Each one of them has to send me a letter in which he says, and I quote:
I (or my Minister)-
If it is the Executive Assistant.
-request the use of this aircraft fully cognizant of the guidelines established by the Department of Transport, consistent with the Government's commitment to restraint and the Prime Minister's code of conduct as applied to Ministers of the Crown.

June 2, 1983
Oral Questions
He must sign that, and then it is his responsibility to justify and answer questions of the type which has just been posed.

CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS

speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext: And in this regard, to avoid the boondoggling as much as possible with respect to Canadian National Railways' further investment of Canadian taxpayers' dollars in Cast, and to avoid what we are learning more and more about every day the fiasco with the Challenger, with Canadair, the $1.5 billion-

Madam Speaker, a decision has not been made, so, consequently, my colleagues in the Cabinet, having listened to the question, can decide to take the factors mentioned into consideration. At least some of them have already been taken into consideration. However, I can only say that the merger of Cast and CN is a commercial deal. If one waits until one goes to the CTC to get an authorization of some kind, one may wait a long time, first of all because it takes time to make the decision and, second, it

subtopic: NUCLEAR ENERGY
NUCLEAR ENERGY
subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION AND STORAGE OF ONTARIO HYDRO NUCLEAR WASTES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. As the Minister knows, Ontario Hydro has stored millions of gallons of radioactive water at Pickering as part of the waste from its atomic energy reactor, part of the disastrous nuclear power program which has placed Ontario Hydro and the people of Ontario into $16 billion of debt.
As the Minister also knows, Ontario Hydro has recently announced that, in order to cut out the cost of a treatment plant, which it promised after some of this radioactive water leaked into Lake Ontario four years ago, it will transport this dangerous radioactive poison, in the equivalent of a truckload every second day, through Ajax, Whitby, and Oshawa, to Port Darlington. Will the Minister, the toothless watchdog of the Atomic Energy Control Board, today give this House a commitment to stop Ontario Hydro from endangering present and future generations of Canadians, and to provide the money necessary to treat nuclear waste safely?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

Madam Speaker, government directives have been issued regarding safety procedures for these materials, and Hydro Ontario is obliged to follow them. We intend to ensure
June 2, 1983

that the regulations concerning the disposal of nuclear waste are observed, in this case as in any other.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF NUCLEAR ENERGY COSTS
REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF NUCLEAR ENERGY COSTS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, since the Minister has not seriously answered the question, I would like to ask him a further question. Since he seems willing to risk the safety of millions of Canadians, not only with radioactive water but with radioactive spent nuclear fuel and radioactive mine tailings, will he now tell us the true total cost of the Government's nuclear power program, including the cost of waste treatment? If he does not know the answer to that, will he at last heed the call of church leaders, union officers, and community spokespersons, by establishing a public inquiry into the risks and costs of the whole nuclear production cycle from mining to waste disposal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF NUCLEAR ENERGY COSTS

Madam Speaker, to answer the question in terms of the cost, I cannot give the Hon. Member that answer because he did not give me any notice. I will certainly look into it. If he would ask his question in a proper fashion, it would be put on the Order Paper and we would reply to it.
In terms of the inquiry, there were many inquiries on that subject, and I do feel that the performance of the Canadian nuclear atomic energy industry has been probably the safest in the world. We have never encountered any serious accident in Canada. We have developed a very good safe system, the Candu reactor. We have some mines which operate in the uranium fields, and so on. There is in Canada a nuclear energy policy which is one of the best in the world, and I am not ashamed of it.

subtopic: TRANSPORTATION REGULATIONS
TRANSPORTATION REGULATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my further supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Three years ago in July, Parliament passed the Minister's Bill on the transportation of dangerous goods, but the Minister has not yet put any of the regulations under the Bill into force. Will he therefore tell this House today when he will put these regulations into force, and whether these regulations will control the transportation by Ontario Hydro of dangerous nuclear wastes, so as to protect the people of Canada from danger to life and health through irresponsible cost cutting by provincial and federal Governments?

subtopic: TRANSPORTATION REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the value and beauty of the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act which the House passed two years ago is that it is all-encompassing. It covers federal and provincial jurisdictions alike, which is an innovation in the federal system in Canada-a very good one, I feel. Indeed, we have had difficulties in producing the regulations. We are still working at it. The difficulties are many, one of which is that we are trying to reconcile in this set of regulations the development of

this matter in the world today, in Canada-U.S. trade relationships, and so on. It is very, very complex. Drafting is done in full consultation with industry. Progress is being made. Already Unit 1 of these regulations has been gazetted. Units 2 and 3 are coming. I recognize that my Department is late on this subject and I beg indulgence in view of the size, the magnitude, and complexity of the task.

RAILWAYS

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I remember reading that this is a good project that normally would have been approved. LABOUR RELATIONS

June 2, 1983

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we regret very much that both parties to this particular dispute have not shown any sign of compromise or of trying to reach agreement. It is particularly regrettable that they have now broken off all discussion.
I want to point out to the Hon. Member that the right of collective bargaining is an essential right in the whole area of labour-market development. With that right there comes a responsibility to the parties to the collective bargaining. It is very clear in this case that labour and management must exercise their responsibility, not only to themselves but to the public interest. They should get back to the table and bargain for an agreement between themselves as collective bargaining requires them to do.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION
GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same Minister. Since this imminent strike or lockout comes at a very critical time, the crop year end, and having regard to the fact that there was a disruption of a shipment of one million tonnes caused by a strike last Fall, is the Minister saying that he is going to allow a strike or lockout to occur before any action is taken? Why will the Government not take its responsibility and ensure that grain moves in an orderly manner and without disruption?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am not sure that the policy of the Hon. Member's Party is because it is difficult to determine its policy on anything these days. Our policy is very clear. For years we have believed in collective bargaining as the basic means by which we arrive at solutions to labour disputes. We also believe that in order to ensure the trust of collective bargaining we must put the onus on the parties to the dispute to arrive at settlements and to take into account that the full right of the public interest must be served. Of course we want a settlement, and of course we do not want disruption. We believe that the parties to the conflict must get back to the table and bargain in good faith.

subtopic: INDUSTRY
INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. As he knows, the steel industry in Canada is in a pretty chaotic state compared even to some segments of the United States. In my riding, Lake Ontario Steel Company Limited has been operating at 30 per cent capacity and recently increased that to 40 per cent capacity because the inventory depletion.
In view of the fact that the two associated plants of Lake Ontario Steel in New Jersey and in Dallas are working at 100 per cent capacity, and the plant in Whitby is working at 40 per cent capacity, with 400 people unemployed, what action is the Government taking in order to give some security to the steel industry and getting employees back to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: INDUSTRY
speechtext:
June 2, 1983

Madam Speaker, first of all the cyclical problem that the Canadian industry is experiencing is no different from that of other industrialized countries. As a matter of fact our steel industry happens to be in better shape than nearly all the industrialized nations of the world. That is mainly because of the capital cost allowances which the federal Government has offered over the past 15 years.
As a matter of fact, Madam Speaker, when the Reagan administration came into power, one of the areas they wanted to look at was the capital cost allowance that the Canadian Liberal Government had introduced, because they wanted to adopt similar measures to ensure that their steel companies were operating at maximum capacity utilization.

SMALL BUSINESS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TAX INCENTIVE TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT

Since small business is by far the largest and most productive potential employer in Canada and is not able to benefit from all the phony and costly temporary make work projects, would the Minister consider initiating or supporting employment tax incentives against unemployment insurance premiums for easier and more extensive hiring by the small business sector, thereby providing more jobs and, more important, more productive jobs?

subtopic: INCENTIVES FOR OIL SANDS PROJECTS
INCENTIVES FOR OIL SANDS PROJECTS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who will know that the development of the oil sands creates thousands of jobs in virtually every sector of the Canadian economy, particularly in central Canada. He will also know that had the same deal been given to Alsands or Shell as was given to BP at Wolf Lake, we would now have an Alsands project going. In the spirit of creating jobs and putting Canadians back to work, is the Minister presently dealing with Shell Oil or Syncrude to see if they can be given the same deal so that they will develop the oil sands in the same way as at Wolf Lake?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: INCENTIVES FOR OIL SANDS PROJECTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are discussing some projects with some sectors of the petroleum industry. I am not at liberty to name the companies. There are some projects being debated at this time. Of course one of the problems is that many of the projects in the past were based on an ever-increasing international price for oil. We see now that the price has gone down so the economics of these projects are not the same as they were two years ago.
Most of the difficulties are not because of the tax propositions we have put forward. The Wolf Lake project was accepted not long ago. Many of the difficulties are not because of a lack of tax incentives from the federal Government or royalty incentives from the Alberta Government; they are based on the international price of oil which is not going up but is going down at this time.

companies for the development of the oil sands in exactly the same way it was offered to BP and Petro-Canada?

subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING PENALTIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member had the opportunity, if she so desired, to direct all of her questions to the Chairman of the CRTC, who appeared in front of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture of the House. During the course of his presentation there, the Chairman of the CRTC, himself, indicated that he thought the proper place for dealing with obscenity in Canada was through the Criminal Code.
Very recently the Minister of Justice of Canada indicated his intentions of bringing forward amendments to the obscenity provisions of the Criminal Code of Canada. The basic position of the Government of Canada is that problems of obscenity on TV or in other areas should be dealt with, as is also stated in the Broadcasting Act, by a statute of general application. The statute of general application which should apply in such a situation is, indeed, the Criminal Code of Canada.
It ought not to be up to the Crown, the Government, or the executive, to decide what type of programming ought to be allowed in the broadcasting system in Canada. To make that type of suggestion is to indicate that we should have the type of system which does indeed exist in many socialist countries, but which does not exist in countries such as Canada.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take part in the debate on second reading of this important Bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is clear that in the circumstances, the Bill must be passed today, and I am sure that all Canadians will be glad to hear that we have been able to obtain the co-operation of the Opposition parties and will therefore be able to pass all three stages of the Bill this afternoon.
Mr. Speaker, in 1977, when the Government introduced variable criteria for eligibility for unemployment insurance and decided that these criteria could vary according to region, it realized that the unemployment problem was not the same everywhere in Canada, and that is why periods varying from ten to fourteen weeks were introduced, depending on the unemployment rate in the region concerned. Mr. Speaker, this Bill is intended to confirm the use of these variable criteria
June 2, 1983

during the next two years, and I would like to emphasize that it is absolutely vital in regions like ours. I am particularly pleased, in this connection, to be able to draw the attention of the House to a group of senior citizens from the Municipality of Carleton, who can appreciate the advantages of this legislation.
Most of these people have experienced very difficult periods in their lives at a time when there was no legislation to protect them when unemployment was high and it was impossible for them to get a job. That is why the Government has decided to extend the period from sixty-six months to ninety, a measure that was urgently needed in our region and all other regions in Canada.
Of course, if we had agreed to proposals urging the Government to apply the same standard of fourteen weeks across the country, the Government would have saved about $500 million, but in view of the present situation across Canada and the unemployment rate, the Government has decided to maintain the variable criteria and to let some 100,000 workers continue to benefit from the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Mr. Speaker, we have also made other changes which are extremely important to many, many workers across the country and which have a direct impact on the region I represent in the House of Commons.
We want to make it possible for the Government to establish regulations that will help fishermen. I have already had an opportunity to draw the attention of the House to a very unfortunate situation existing today in the Magdalen Islands, in my riding, and I think it is very sad that the Quebec Government cannot set aside its political ideology so that we can settle this problem. The fishermen will understand and realize that the changes we want to make in the Unemployment Insurance Act will make it possible for many of them to extend their fishing season for up to two or three weeks and sometimes up to a month, because these changes will not affect their insurable earnings. They will be able to receive unemployment insurance benefits during the winter months and sometimes during the summer as well, which will guarantee them a decent income.
In recent years, and especially in recent months, I have been meeting a number of fishermen's associations in the Gaspe, in the Magdalen Islands, on the North Shore, on the Lower North Shore and even in wellknown fishing areas in New Brunswick and other parts of the Maritime Provinces, and most of these fishermen, if not all, were in favour of the changes that we are proposing today. That is why we are proceeding with this legislation and why we want to give fishermen-Mr. Speaker, I am referring to people who work as fishermen on a boat-better opportunities for working at their own occupation.
Unemployment Insurance Act
The changes we want to introduce will, as I said earlier, enable the Commission to prepare regulations that will give the fishermen far greater flexibility.
In recent years, and especially last summer, I noticed in my riding that people have had to give up fishing because it was not worthwhile for them to continue fishing during the last weeks of August, September or October, because of weather conditions. When a fisherman wants to go out to sea on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday and there is a storm, he will certainly not go out on Thursday or Friday, because his catch for those two days will be so limited as to have a direct impact on his insurable earnings.
The changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act will enable the Minister to implement the recommendation in the Kirby report that the fisherman's ten best weeks during the fishing season should be used to establish his eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits and the amount of such benefits.
In my view, these changes are very important, and I am sure that the Opposition Parties have also realized that they were urgently needed in order to help people make a decent living during the fishing season, which has already started.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not make further demands on the time of the House, and these are the two points I wanted to make with respect to the Bill being considered today. I am sure that all Canadians, and especially people living in Eastern Quebec and the Maritime Provinces, will realize that in proposing these amendments, the Government has firmly resolved to remove regional disparities in our country and to enable all Canadians, wherever they may live, to have a share of the wealth in this country, and to be able to make a decent living and have the same standard of living wherever they may be.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to congratulate the Minister and thank him for bringing in the adoptive parents amendment. Some weeks ago when this Bill was before us in Committee of the Whole, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and I brought this matter to the attention of the Minister and he appeared sympathetic at that time. I am very pleased indeed that he has now brought in this amendment. I do not think that we recognize enough the service that parents give to the country in adopting children. Many of these children have no name and no prospects except that of living in foster homes or institutions. Adoptive parents give the child a name and he or she becomes part of the family with all its advantages. Most important, the child is given training by the parents and starts out on an equal basis with other boys and girls.
Until this time this legislation has been very discriminatory. Some time ago the lawmakers saw fit to give consideration to the natural mother of a child in collecting unemployment insurance benefits if she qualified. That was an excellent piece

June 2, 1983
Unemployment Insurance Act
of legislation also. When difficulties and complications during birth arise, sometimes the six month period is not enough. 1 understand the amendments which are going to be proposed this afternoon will look after that situation, and that where there are complications a mother who qualifies will then be able to have that time extended a reasonable amount. I am looking forward to seeing that amendment.
When Parliament adopted that Section to provide unemployment insurance for natural mothers, Mr. Speaker, it did not provide the same benefit for adoptive parents. Many Provinces, certainly Alberta, require that one of the adoptive parents must remain home with the child for a period of six months. In many cases this is tantamount to giving birth to the child because the child is adopted two or three days, sometimes seven days, after its birth. I think the agencies across this country concerned with child welfare who have followed that practice were acting wisely and in the interests of the child. I think it was one of the Holy Fathers who said if he had the care of the child for the first seven years, then he did not worry too much about that child after that. I think generally that is true and that is the basis, I believe, of the thinking of our welfare departments when they say parents who adopt a child should remain at home with that child for a period of six months. I hope there will be some provision made for that too.
What has happened until now, Mr. Speaker, is that there has been no unemployment insurance for adoptive parents. Consequently, they had to leave their jobs, and sometimes it was not there when they wanted to go back. With today's cost of living, many of these parents ran into financial difficulties because they were used to the two pay cheques coming into the home. When that is cut back to one, then they have financial difficulties. I understand that some provincial Ministers concerned, certainly in Alberta, have looked with a good deal of compassion on cases like that and have ensured that the parents could go back to work. However, there were other times when the job would be lost if the parents could not go back to work. Now that is no longer going to be a problem because if the mother qualifies for unemployment insurance, then she will be able to draw unemployment insurance just as if she was a natural mother. I think that is excellent, and again, as I said at the beginning, I want to commend the minister for bringing in this amendment. He could have said, "We are too busy now. We have many other Bills". Instead, he put this one on the line, he said it was important, and I agree with him. This will have a great impact on scores of babies who are adopted from this time onward because the parent will be able to stay home and give the child the training it requires.
Now when a parent adopts a child of school age the same problem does not exist. Many of our child welfare agencies recognize that. Someone should be at home with the child when he is not at school, but certainly parents can work during school hours without detriment to the child. That is provided for in the rules and regulations of the Province of Alberta, and I suppose in every other Province. Consequently, when a child is adopted at the age of 12 or 14, again the parent should be at home when the child is there. But it is not the same situation as when a family adopts a three-day old baby. So this is
excellent legislation. It will eliminate the discrimination in the Act.
Some of my own constituents have faced that discrimination and they felt it was the officers of the Commission who were preventing them from obtaining unemployment insurance. They could not believe that the law said that only natural parents would secure this benefit. Some even appealed the decisions because they wanted to bring attention to the discrimination which was evident. I am glad that the Bill, with thanks to the Minister who has brought it in at this time, will eliminate discrimination against adoptive parents.
I say again that we owe a tremendous amount to men and women who adopt a baby or child of any age, take the child into their home, make it their own, and provide it with not only worldly goods, clothes and education, but also with love and care. That is one of the important things in a young child's life.
This is important legislation and I am certainly happy that the Minister is presenting it this afternoon. Some people have said to me that there is too much of a chance for abuse in this legislation. I cannot see that. It has been mentioned that some people will pay $5,000 for a baby. Will the mother then be able to collect unemployment insurance? Anyone who pays $5,000, $1,000 or any sum of money to buy a baby is surely in such a good financial position that the mother may not even be working. Such people want a child so badly that they are prepared to buy one. They have the worldly goods. If it is done above board, and I do not like that type of thing myself, but if it is done above the table, through proper authorities, the child does receive a home. However, such a parent would not qualify for unemployment insurance.
The only mothers or fathers who qualify will be those who have the necessary weeks of employment with a particular firm. No one will work just for the sake of being able to draw unemployment insurance after adopting a child. It is part of their lives. They try to build up a home. They try to have a home, a nest, so to speak. Then, when they are in a sufficiently good financial position to give a child a worth-while life, they adopt. The everyday expenses are heavy. This is where the unemployment insurance will come in. It will be a tremendous boost to those who qualify for it. For those who do not qualify, it will be exactly the way it is today. There will not be any change. There will not be scores of people who will suddenly adopt babies just for the sake of receiving unemployment insurance benefits. I do not believe that at all. As a matter of fact, there are not that many babies available. They are scarce when one wants to adopt a child. Maybe that is good. However, these people do have to qualify under the Act.
When they qualify, they are entitled to benefits, just the same as a workman who becomes ill on the job. If he has the necessary weeks, he receives the unemployment insurance to which he is entitled. He must have it to continue to live. Today many of our workers do not have nest eggs. They live week by week or month by month, on their paycheques. Therefore, I do
June 2, 1983

not think this will be a tremendous burden on the Unemployment Insurance Fund. I am doubtful if, after a year, we will even notice the amount which is drawn out of the fund by adoptive parents. However, even if we do, this is worthwhile legislation.
It is also necessary for everyone in the country who is contributing to be able to work. Work is necessary. Productivity is necessary. Without productivity in this country, we cannot have legislation such as this. Without productivity, we cannot have old age pensions or care for those who need it the most. Consequently, a central part of this whole program is to ensure more and more industries, investment and employment of people so that employers and workers continue to contribute to the Unemployment Insurance Fund. The productivity in the country enables the Government to give out social legislation such as this which will be of benefit and help to us in the future.
I do not think that a dollar spent on care for a child, whether an adopted child or otherwise, is money lost. I do not think it is an expense. Rather, it is an investment. Every child in whom we invest will make a contribution in the future. More and more, we must start thinking about investing in our boys and girls instead of paying thousands of dollars after they make mistakes. Let us prevent the mistakes from happening. We surely know enough psychology and sociology today to be able to work out plans which will enable scores of boys and girls who today land up in our prisons and institutional homes to have the proper channels to make a go in life so that they do not end up in jail.
I remember going to an institution in Edmonton just a few years ago. I saw many boys and girls, 14 years to 16 years of age, who had been sent there by the courts. When I spoke to many of them, I found that the reason they were there could be summed like this: they did not make their way in high school. They did not learn how to read when they were in grades one through five. They were slow learners. They were pushed ahead until they reached the senior grades of elementary school or the early years of high school. They could not read and could not keep up. They became discouraged and frustrated and dropped out. Then they lost their friends who were still in school. They got in with a bad crowd, and that is why they ended up in the institution.
I saw them trying to learn how to read. One boy was reading a book with the name of a detective story on the cover. I asked the instructor why he was reading detective stories. He said, "That is not a detective story. Go around and look". I did so and found that the boy was reading a grade three primer. He was learning how to read but did not want anyone to know that he did not know how to read, and that was natural. A child should not be embarrassed because he is a slow learner.
Our schools must recognize the fact that our boys and girls who are slow learners are not retarded. They just need extra attention. If they learn how to read, that is one of the best things in the world to ensure that they will make their way in life a little later on. This will prevent us from having to spend money on jails and institutions. Thousands of dollars are being spent today, but this expense could be avoided if we take the
Unemployment Insurance Act
necessary sociological and psychological steps to try to prevent these children from taking the wrong path. We should help them to go on the right path, which will make them better citizens and the country a better country.
Greater productivity will enable us to give good social legislation to the people who need it, including what we are doing today. However, if we do not have productivity, then we will not be able to provide those things we want to provide to those who are unable to provide for themselves, those who are unable to care for themselves, those who need the help the most.
Therefore, I would like to emphasize two points. The Unemployment Insurance Fund is there. If there are abuses, let us try to wipe them out. We should find them and cure them. There are abuses in this type of legislation, but let us not penalize those who only want to do what is right with the fund because there are others who abuse the fund. Second, let us ensure that we give the people of this country a chance to invest, encouraging them to invest their money so that we can have jobs. There are no jobs without investment. Invest the money, and then money will come into funds such as the Unemployment Insurance Fund, enabling us to provide legislation of this kind without its being a burden on the country.
I am happy to see this legislation coming in. It is long overdue. It is doing away with discrimination which should never have been there but has been there. It will now make many people across the country happy because they can see that they may well be able to adopt a child, whereas before they just could not afford to do it.

The Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) just said that that is not true. After the argument that occurred this morning, I would advise the Hon. Member not to say that. It leads to all kinds of procedural harangues.
With respect to the previous amendments to the Bill, I do not mind admitting that there was a fair amount of debate not only between the two sides of the House but in the caucuses. If the other caucuses reacted in any way similar to the Liberal caucus at the time, there must have been a lot of debate within the caucuses. I remember very well a number of meetings which we had with the then Minister in which we from the Atlantic Liberal caucus not only proposed but demanded that there be variable entrance requirements. The Hon. Member for St. John's East says that that was after he put it forward. If it was after he put it forward, that is fine with me. We won the day and we have variable entrance requirements.
The principle being argued at that time, which was not really a principle but an expediency, was that certain people from certain parts of the country, without naming them specifically, which were heavily industrialized and well developed, wanted to cut the guts out of the unemployment insurance system at the time and make it much more difficult for people to get on the unemployment insurance rolls. They were very enthusiastic about making it much tougher for people to draw unemployment insurance. Some of us who represent areas that are not quite as well developed and do not have all the facilities and industry that other areas have, stood our ground and said that they cannot legislate for the industrialized parts of the country alone. As a result of that objection we now have the variable entrance provisions in the Bill.
I wish to say something about the Minister. I believe most Members of the House would agree that the Minister is a very responsible and responsive Minister. He has taken his duties seriously and has worked very hard to mitigate the effects of the recession which we have experienced in this country. He has designed programs to put people back to work. He has listened carefully, reacted quickly and has used every means at his disposal to consult not only with his colleagues in the front
benches but with all of his colleagues in the House to make life better for the people whom we represent. I want to take this opportunity to thank him publicly.
There are three very important areas in the Bill and most of them have been spoken to. I want to add my support for the provision of equal treatment for women whether they are natural or adoptive parents. I believe that to be an extremely important measure. Another extremely important provision is the variable entrance requirements which are extended by this Bill. That is particularly important to areas of high unemployment in this country.
This morning we heard a lot of rhetoric about fishermen from the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper). He talked about the fact that there were no amendments in this Bill dealing with fishermen. While there is no doubt that amendments are needed, everyone knows that this is what might be termed emergency legislation to prevent a sunset clause on the variable entrance requirements coming into effect. I am not convinced that amendments to the fisheries provision in the Unemployment Insurance Act at this time would receive the proper scrutiny in order to ensure that the best possible provisions are made for that vital industry in Atlantic Canada, the Pacific Coast and also the inland waters of Canada.
While the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James was doing a great job this morning of straddling both the issues of motherhood and apple pie, and wept eloquently, I must point out that he failed to mention that fishermen are in fact the only self employed people in the country who have access to the unemployment insurance scheme. He also talked about the need to lower the premiums, the Government's obligation to provide a job for everyone, and the need to pay for unemployment insurance out of general revenue. That is great socialist pap, but that is the best that can be said for it.
He talked about the degradation of welfare. I cannot see the degradation of welfare, and such a term should not be attached to it. If there is a degradation of welfare it is a result of how the Provinces have administered it. What the Hon. Member proposes to do with the unemployment insurance scheme would make it nothing more than an extension of the welfare system. In my opinion, to follow that kind of facile proposal would result in the destruction of the unemployment insurance scheme. It would no longer be an employment insurance scheme, as it should be called, but simply an extension of welfare. It would be another welfare system operated by the Government of Canada rather than by the Governments of the Provinces.
Before I sit down, there is one plea I want to make to the Minister. I think the greatest problem with unemployment insurance in the country is the determination of eligibility. We have literally hundreds of cases, probably thousands across the country, where eligibility or ineligibility is determined after the fact rather than before the fact. Claimants are sometimes told
June 2, 1983

that they must pay back thousands of dollars to the federal Treasury after they have received the payments in good faith, because it is not the Unemployment Commission that is determining eligibility, it is the Department of National Revenue, a Department that is known to have all the subtlety of the wreckers' ball. It is absolutely imperative in my opinion that that determination of eligibility be done by the Commission within the Department of Employment and Immigration where there is some sensitivity to the unemployed and knowledge of whether or not a person is eligible for unemployment insurance.
There are other regulations surrounding unemployment insurance that are counter productive as well, and I think we have to take a look at those. For example, there is the provision that prevents the person receiving unemployment insurance from going to school, trade school or some other institution of learning to take courses to advance his or her ability to find a job.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak briefly to this Bill. Before speaking to the Bill specifically, I want to associate myself with the remarks of the Hon. Member for Northumber-land-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) with respect to the current practice under the regulations of the unemployment insurance office in Orillia and Midland, clamping down with vengeance unseen anywhere else upon poor, unsuspecting constituents of mine who are laid off. Of their own volition they took a course and then found that the bureaucratic weight of the unemployment Insurance Commission came crashing down on them. Because the Commission cannot find them a job, because they had the gumption and the initiative to take a course to improve themselves, the bureaucrats in the Commission can find them unavailable for work and they are cut off unemployment insurance payments.
I share with the Hon. Member for Northumberland-Miramichi the abhorrence for this system and regulation. I urge the Minister to take a hard look at Canadians in every constituency who are trying to improve themselves and cannot find work. They find that the bureaucrats have an answer when they go to take a course, but no answer when it comes to finding a job.
I am pleased to speak to this Bill because for some time it has bothered me that discrimination exists in the present legislation whereby parents of adopted children do not have the same rights as natural parents. This Bill will change that. It will eliminate discrimination against an adoptive parent. Also, and I am in favour of this, it will repeal the rule which states that a woman must have worked ten weeks around the time of conception to be eligible for benefits. It will repeal the section which prevents a pregnant woman from getting regular benefits or sickness benefits in the weeks surrounding the birth of a child.
I support that concept entirely. In 1982 I moved a motion under Standing Order 43 on the floor of the House. I urged the Government to adopt the recommendations of the Task Force on Unemployment Insurance which came down in July, 1981. I said that in the interest of equity and fairness, maternity benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act should be
Unemployment Insurance Act
extended to newly adoptive parents. Parents who adopt children face the same physical, mental, social and economic adjustments as natural parents. They often do not have advance notice of the date of adoption. I am pleased the Government has finally brought in this legislation to correct that discrimination.
I have received letters on this. The interest comes from my riding. In 1980 I received a letter from a person in Orillia who felt that it was unfair and discriminatory that adoptive parents do not have the same privileges as natural parents. The St. Columbkille's Catholic Women's League has urged me to push this. They state that as far as that organization is concerned, adoptive parents should receive maternity benefits under unemployment insurance in the same way as natural parents. I put this on the record knowing that in Ontario, the Children's Aid Society requires that adoptive parents have six months to get used to parenthood, taking care of an adopted child and helping to bring about the natural family. I have talked with several friends who have adopted children. I know there is an adjustment period much the same as any natural parent goes through.
I spoke only to those parts of the Bill which are of concern to me. They are the ones I have mentioned. My Party is in favour of this legislation. I am pleased that the Government has finally seen fit to eliminate this discrimination which should never have occurred.

It is true that that provision had been unfair to some women, particularly those who had been working for some time and were unfortunately forced to change jobs. They were left in a difficult situation.
The repeal of the provisions of Section 46 is the second good news. Under that section, women were not eligible for unemployment insurance benefits, including standard benefits or sickness benefits for a given period of time. On the basis of a

June 2, 1983
Unemployment Insurance Act
fancy formula, it had been decided that pregnant women would not be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits between the eighth and sixth weeks before the expected delivery date. The United Fishermen's Allied Workers' Union in British Columbia, the largest union representing fishermen, is very concerned about this legislation. I think that its concern stems from its understanding of the Bill's implications in the short time in which it had access to this Bill. Fishermen have not had the opportunity to meet with their organizations and look at the implications of these amendments, nor have they had the opportunity to make representations to the Unemployment Insurance Commission or any parliamentary committee about the concerns that they have been expressing for a number of years. I believe that those concerns must be expressed, but because of the shortened length of debate time for this Bill and because it is very important that some of the provisions in it are passed before June 4, fishermen will not be afforded the opportunity to have the input that they require in order to meet some of their concerns.
One concern that I think I share with the fishermen is that in the fishing industry at this time, an industry which is under a certain amount of pressure in terms of fishing, particularly on the West Coast, the length of the fishing season is being shortened all the time. That is in regard to conserving stocks and the amount of time in which people are allowed to fish. The amount of time that shore workers have to work in plants is being shortened all the time. Yet we see no indication that the entrance requirements for fishermen will be reduced.
Fishermen in British Columbia have made representations to the Government in the past to reduce the required number of weeks to eight weeks if possible, and there has been no indication that the regulations will deal with this concern. It is a sincere concern that fishermen have. Not only do they have a
June 2, 1983

restricted season, but as we on both coasts know, they are also limited by the kind of weather that they can work in, by breakdowns in equipment, and by scarcity of fish. These limitations do not allow fishermen the time necessary to qualify for benefits. Both on the East Coast and the West Coast the obvious concern will be for the number of weeks that will be required to qualify for unemployment insurance.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) represents the inland waters area and has indicated that there is going to be some change in the regulations which will affect the incomes of fishermen in Manitoba and Saskatchewan who are winter fishermen and therefore do not come under the normal fishing season from March to November. Now, in June, 1983, we have a promise that fishermen's concerns will be met. This Party is not satisfied that promises through regulations are something that we can put faith in. Despite what the Conservative Party may feel, we think some things should be changed in the Bill to guarantee fishermen access to unemployment insurance at any time of the year, whether in the winter season or what is the normal season for most Canadian fishermen, and those weeks should be considered as insurable weeks for UIC benefits. We have other recommendations to move which will allow fishermen to collect unemployment insurance benefits for any period of the year during which they have an insurable claim. They find that they are able to collect only six weeks, and then when they get into the normal fishing season they are disqualified despite having paid into the fund over the winter months.
We are not pleased that this portion of the Bill was introduced in this way. There are some very serious and sincere concerns in the fishing industry. They have only had two weeks to react to this proposal and in many cases have had no opportinunity to meet with their membership because they are out fishing.
Because there is so little time for debate, we would like to see these provisions proceed expeditiously. I suggest that the Government and the Official Opposition look seriously at the
Unemployment Insurance Act
changes in the Act so that fishermen are satisfied that they would be protected in insurable weeks and benefit weeks.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-156 has given us an opportunity to discuss a number of important questions in connection with the Unemployment Insurance Program. I am supporting this Bill because I believe it will improve conditions for many unemployment insurance recipients, and I am pleased to see that we have the consent of the House today for passing all stages of the Bill.
Regarding the changes proposed by the Kirby Task Force with respect to unemployment insurance premiums paid by fishermen, the Bill will enable the Government to make regulations authorizing fishermen to select the 10 best weeks among the 15 weeks in which they earn income from fishing in order to calculate their average earnings for the purposes of unemployment insurance benefits. 1 agree with this recommendation, but I believe that the recommendation by the Kirby Task Force is not entirely satisfactory because it does not mention the effect it will have on workers in fish processing factories. I realize it is impossible in the latter case to change the Act as quickly as in the case of fishermen, because there, the statutory basis of the Unemployment Insurance Program is entirely different, and changes can be made by Order in Council or by a single Cabinet decision. If we want to change anything that concerns ordinary unemployment, we must change the Act according to the same procedure followed in other cases. However, I suppose the Minister is aware of this point, because workers in fish processing plants have been complaining for a long time, and I know that Members on all sides of the House who have fish processing plants in their ridings, as well as related industries, are aware that usually in the fall, especially in the case of herring and groundfish when

June 2, 1983
Unemployment Insurance Act
the catch situation is either feast or famine, workers in fish processing plants-even before these changes-were losing a lot on their unemployment insurance benefits because they were sometimes on and then off again for two or three days, and this was on a very irregular basis. At the end of the season, when the weather was bad, and especially in the case of herring and groundfish caught along the coast, not by big trawlers, in the case of groundfish, but along the coast, especially with gill nets or lines, processing plant workers could expect a drop in their average earnings which would then be reflected in their unemployment insurance benefits throughout the winter.
Although the proposed changes will improve the situation for fishermen by letting them select their 10 best weeks out of 15, there will be no benefit to processing plant workers and fishermen on the contrary. I say this because fishermen will now have an incentive to go out, and that is all right, even if they can only do so one or two days a week if the weather has been bad, while the worker in the processing plant will be called back to work to process the fish, and as a result, he is going to be worse off. I raised this matter with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), and I hope he will soon proceed with a study of the impact this will have on fish processing plants and that it will not be long before changes will be introduced which, I feel, should not necessarily apply only to the fishing industry. I know that the same problem exists in other industries that are affected by weather, such as peat harvesting and sometimes the lumber industry, especially when there have been extensive forest fires. I would like to see the Act changed to allow the Minister some flexibility in designating, in certain cases, specific industries or regions where there has been a particular weather problem or when there has been a forest fire or a dry spell in the forest that has prevented lumberjacks from working for extended periods of time. Mr. Speaker, there is another problem which I will have to mention, although it is not the subject-matter of this Bill. I share the concern which the Hon. Member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) and other Hon. Members have expressed about the problem of "assurability" of the job under the existing legislation. On several occasions, I have discussed this problem with the Minister which I feel is both very serious and complex especially because there are some 27 or 28 applicants in my riding who have appealed the negative decisions rendered in their case, construction workers doing minor housing repairs; their "assurability" has been questioned after the fact by the Department of National Revenue, in some cases up to three years after the employment had been terminated. The result is that after many appeals at various stages, they are still faced with "overpayments".
I should like to remind the House of a decision which was rendered on February 6, 1980 by Hon. Justice Dubinsky, a current judge of the Federal Court of Canada, at a time when he was sitting as an umpire to deal with the appeal of a Mr. Childs, from Western Bay, Conception Bay, in Newfoundland. Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote part of Justice Dubinsky's
decision, for it implies that we have a moral responsibility in connection with this matter and I quote:
The Appellant has been overpaid to a large amount. He is married and has four children, three of whom are in school. He owns his home at Western Bay, Conception Bay, Newfoundland, but he has no bonds, securities of any sort and his bank account does not exceed $200.00. I am satisfied beyond any doubt that to have him repay the overpayment would cause undue hardship for him and his family. 1, therefore, feel that consideration should be given to him under the provisions of Section 175(1 )(e)(ii) of the Regulations, particularly since he was allowed to receive benefits for a long time-
This is where the moral obligation comes in, Mr. Speaker.
-without there being question and, moreover, because his actions herein were not deliberately done to defraud the Commission.
The judge goes on to indicate that the Commission has the authority to write off these payments but that it has been impossible because of the present law. I am told that if it did this, it would mean that many overpayments by the Government would also go uncollected. I am not sure that the other overpayments by the Government have the same effect on people. Any Hon. Member from a rural area of the country has lived with this problem, I am told by a lot of them, and the Minister has looked at different options as to how we could solve this problem.
The Hon. Member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) has suggested that the whole question of insurability should come back under the law to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I could live with that. However, I am told that that creates incredible problems. The Minister has agreed in a personal conversation with me-and I would ask all Hon. Members to support this initiative-to refer this whole question of insurability of employment to the committee, either the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, or a special committee of the House, with a short term of reference, in order that Hon. Members can deal with this problem and come up with an option which would be acceptable.
The effect of this, Mr. Speaker, is that people have had their eligibility or insurability of employment questioned after the fact. They were working for an employer in an activity which they thought was legitimate and which they thought was insurable. They then found out that it was not. The employer is home free. He has no responsibility under the law. But the claimant then is classified as not having been in an insurable employment, and all of the benefits he has received become due and payable to the Government as an overpayment. In order to have them written off, according to the present law, one has to show "undue hardship", and that is practically impossible. To prove undue hardship under the present law one would have to lose everything he or she has. This is not acceptable.
It is incredible that we would have a system which would let this kind of thing go on. In my view, when a person is working

bona fide, and when it is shown that there was no attempt to defraud the Commission-because in some cases there are, inevitably-in no way should these people be asked, threatened or told that they owe money to the Crown, as in the case of the decision of Judge Dubinsky who said there was no attempt to defraud the Commission. If the person was well intentioned, the employer was well intentioned, and they both thought the employment was insurable, then the system should accept the responsibility of that and the onus should not be on the worker, post factum, two or three years after the fact to prove that he or she was eligible.
