subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to take part in this debate on improvements to the unemployment insurance system. I recall having lobbied the current Minister, and indeed other Ministers, on the particular aspects of maternity benefits, which is
Unemployment Insurance Act
what I want to address today. I remember lobbying even a Conservative Minister on this subject, and it is pleasant to see that resistance eventually declined until we finally moved to the stage of receiving acceptance in principle. Then the issue stalled while the committee examined the question, but now we actually have the legislation.
First of all, let me deal with the subject of adoptive parents. We are all very pleased to see these new measures. Our Party has urged them for years, and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), recently had his Private Members' Bill on this issue debated. The measures are long overdue and we are very pleased to see them.
One of the good provisions is that either parent can take leave to look after the new child. Most of the time the leave will probably be taken by the mother, but the option is there for the father. However, what is not yet in the legislation is the possibility of the leave being shared by both parents. There are of course many couples where the child care tasks could be shared by both and the parents would prefer to do it that way. Our system is still unduly rigid in this respect and it is something which should be amended. It is a concern of the women's movement that life be better organized to allow for the combination of paid work and child care. In the long term we want to see a shorter work week so that both parents can do this. In the question immediately before us of adoptive leave, surely it would be very reasonable to see that both parents could share in that work. We should be facilitating the sharing of child care between parents when they want it.
This Bill, Mr. Speaker, eliminates a number of discriminatory sections which should never have been law in the first place and which have been an embarrassment to women. A large number of women were actually denied claims because of the additional requirements they had to meet to get maternity benefits. The magic ten rule is one that we are all very pleased to see go. It has taken a long time. It was based on a very insulting view of women in the first place, that an unemployed woman was sitting around idle until she became pregnant, and then went out to get a job so she would be able to take maternity leave. That is probably something which never happened in the first place and certainly should not have been the basis for legislation. It is very good to see that section go.
There will be more flexibility in the claim period. This is certainly a very welcome reform. The prediction of delivery dates is of course always difficult. Babies sometimes have their own timetables which do not coincide with those of their doctors or, indeed, of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. So we are pleased to see this new flexibility in the legislation.
The discriminatory provisions in Section 46, which did not allow women to claim regular unemployment insurance or sickness benefits during the period of pregnancy or after birth is of course something that should never have been in the legislation. We are very pleased to see it go. This is the Section

June 2, 1983
Unemployment Insurance Act
that Stella Bliss claimed was discriminatory under the Canadian Bill of Rights. She lost her claim. 1 do not think we can discuss Bill C-156 without remembering and indeed saluting Stella Bliss. The Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald) has recounted some of the judicial horrors of this case. It is certainly a model of erroneous judicial reasoning and should be required reading for future judges in our courts. It will go down with Murdoch, the Person's case, Lavalle and Bedard as horrors that Canadians ought to be embarrassed about.
Let me just recall a few points in this case, Mr. Speaker, Bliss first lost her case to a board of referees, but she won on appeal on a ruling by a federal court judge who was sitting as an umpire under the Unemployment Insurance Act. The Attorney General then appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal. So here we see our own Government's Department of Justice appealing a case of unequal rights of women. We have had far too many cases of this before, and we are hoping that with the new Charter of Rights the Government will defend women in equality cases and not work against them. The case then went up to the Federal Court of Appeal and finally up to the Supreme Court of Canada. It was only decided in 1978, so it is not a long time ago. I think it is important for us to keep these cases in mind. We still have to watch both our courts and the Ministry of Justice.

Mrs. Stella Bliss should be congratulated and thanked for suing the Government for the discriminatory measures against women with unemployment insurance and maternity leave. Unfortunately, Mrs. Bliss lost her claim. The Supreme Court of Canada ruled that it was not the law that discriminated against women, but nature, itself, as though pregnancy were a sickness and even a chronic illness that prevented women from working. After that ruling, the women's movement in Canada fought against this discriminatory legislation and feminist groups called for the elimination of those discriminatory measures. As can be seen today, their lobbying was successful. It took us years, but we have won!

However, what remains? We need a comprehensive parental leave scheme. Indeed, a recent poll showed that 61 per cent of Canadians are in favour of fully paid maternity leave. That is certainly something we have not reached as yet. We need a comprehensive scheme with both a longer number of paid weeks, with options for unpaid leave as well, and a higher rate of pay. In the meantime, further modest improvements could certainly be advanced. We could eliminate the two weeks waiting period, for example. This is an anomaly in the case of maternity leave. It is there to encourage an unemployed worker to go out immediately and look for a job. It is wholly inappropriate in the case of someone expecting to have a child or who has just recently given birth. This would cost money, and therefore it is not possible for the Opposition to move an amendment, but it is something which should be addressed.
Another loophole in the law which affects women is that a woman cannot claim maternity benefits if she is on strike. Her union could go on strike the day before she gives birth, for
example, and she would be disentitled to maternity benefits. That is very inappropriate in her circumstances.
However, there is another reform which would not add to the costs and on which we should act today. That would be to permit either parent to take leave after the birth of the child. Clearly only women can give birth, but after the birth the father could be looking after the child, or both parents could be looking after the child. A growing number of couples do want to these responsibilities, and we should be introducing this flexibility into the legislation.
[ Translation]
Some parents want to share the responsibility of caring for their children. This is allowed in several European countries, such as Sweden and Finland. After the birth of the child, either the father or the mother can take parental leave or both parents can share it. Why not in Canada? We are not suggesting an extension of such leave, but rather a reform, and what we are suggesting will cost nothing. The matter of further improvements to the system is something else that will require the co-operation of the federal and provincial Governments as well as unions and employers. We do not intend to deal with this issue today, but we hope that the Government will address it. For the moment, why not support the useful and reasonable reforms we are suggesting, such as allowing both parents to share the parental leave?

My Party will be presenting amendments in Committee of the Whole on this point. We support the amendments the Government has introduced today. They are welcome and we are very pleased to see them. We hope the Government and the Conservatives as well will support the amendments we will be introducing.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am more than pleased today to have the opportunity to add my comments to the debate on Bill C-156 and to discuss some of the necessary amendments that will bring about a greater equity with respect to claimants qualifying for unemployment insurance benefits.
The basic concept of unemployment insurance, the original program, was established in 1940 and was designed to do two things, first, to provide income protection for workers suffering temporary income interruptions and, second, to facilitate the best possible match between unemployed workers and available jobs. In other words, it was designed to promote the economic and social security of workers. It was recognized that the employed needed to have a greater sense of security, a safety net to safeguard against the dehumanizing effects of the Great Depression. I was indeed very fortunate, because of my age, not to have experienced the frustration, hunger and helplessness faced by millions of people all around the world during the Depression. No one should ever have to be faced with those hardships again but, unfortunately, millions of people are faced with them. In the very grave economic times
June 2, 1983

at present, one sees how this legislation has been most effective in helping these people.
Since the Great Depression, Canada's economic capacity grew and became more stable. The increase in the labour force was meeting the expanding needs of industry. As our population grew, the demand for goods and services also grew. It seemed that this enphoria of economic growth would be never-ending. Unfortunately, this was not the case. Canada's economy has been on a steady decline, to the point at which we are in the midst of the worse recession since those dark days of the Depression. Over this past decade, as a direct result of Canada's economic demise brought on by a Government which felt it could spend with abandon, without any sense of control, there has been the need to meet the ever-increasing demands on the safety nets which were put in place to support Canadians during economic hard times. Amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act comprise just one area where revision has become necessary to meet those demands.
There has been much criticism with respect to the Unemployment Insurance Fund indicating that it has provided a disincentive to workers to seek employment. This criticism might have had some merit in past years, at a time when employment opportunities were plentiful in our economy; but today, at a time when employment has never before been more difficult to find, with unemployment at a rate of over 12 per cent, this criticism does not hold true.
As the economic times change, so has legislation changed to protect the needs of Canada's citizens, be it through the need to encompass a greater degree of flexibility or to provide positive incentives for economic security. Over the past few years, as the country has attempted to weather the economic recession, Canadians have witnessed the effects of a declining labour force. Added to this, we are also confronted with the headlines of the ill effects of high technology, of how this new information society will displace millions of workers in the years ahead no matter how much the economy improves.
We know all too well the burden upon our society of unemployment rates of 12 per cent and 13 per cent, the despair of the unemployed, the rising hopelessness among our youth for whom the rate is already over 20 per cent. We know of the increasing incidence of family violence, alcoholism, delinquency and crime. We dare not contemplate the effects of another 5 per cent unemployed, yet unless we face up to the challenges posed by the new technology, that is precisely what we must expect and be prepared to accept.
There are both threats and opportunities associated with the evolution of the new technology. We have heard warnings of the dangers and the challenges which lie ahead. We must heed those warnings and meet those challenges. This has become more evident with respect to producing the skilled labour and personnel to meet the needs of the new technology.
Statistics have shown that women will be bearing the brunt of the new technology as, more and more, computers replace the jobs currently held by women. We must be prepared to
Unemployment Insurance Act
address the problem by meeting the needs for retraining and education.
The proportion of women in the growth of the labour force increased dramatically from 1940 to 1980, as it became necessary to have two incomes per family and as more women became single parents. We have seen an increase in the number of women in the labour force from under one million in 1940 to almost five million in 1980. Fifty per cent of working age women, those between the ages of 25 to 54, are working, and 66 per cent of those women are married. By 1990, it is expected that 75 per cent of working age women will be in the labour force.
If we consider the historical perspective of women in the labour force, we will see where women have traditionally occupied the lower paying jobs. The service industry, which employs a greater percentage of women than other industries, will be directly affected by the age of technology, and an even greater burden will be placed on the shoulders of women, necessitating the need for economic protection.
We are witnessing change in the roles of the husband and wife as more and more women are being recognized for their valid contributions to society outside the home. Indeed, it is becoming more common to find that the wife is bringing home the larger income and, in some cases, the only income.
We have just come through a decade in which it became increasingly necessary for both partners in the labour force to support the family. With the high cost of mortgages, rents, clothing and food continuing to rise, the burden of providing the necessities of life is falling on the shoulders of women as well as their husbands. Women have also had to enter the labour force out of necessity because many men no longer have the security of permanent, long-term employment. In many areas, such as the mining industry, where hundreds of men were laid off, it has become the responsibility of the wife to bring home the family income.
With these changes in the family structure and the labour force, the need for revisions to existing legislation must be considered in order to keep pace with the demands of a changing society. An area where I feel existing legislation has been most discriminatory and is in need of change involves unemployment insurance benefits with respect to natural and adoptive mothers. The Act does not discriminate with respect to persons in the labour force making contributions to the Unemployment Insurance Fund, requiring that both men and women contribute to the fund in line with their earning capacity. However, the inequity occurs when it becomes necessary to collect benefits from the fund.
Claimants for sick benefits must only prove that they have worked for 20 weeks in the last year, but women applying for maternity benefits are required to meet a set of complex criteria which almost takes a legal mind to understand. At long last, the Government has finally come to terms with the necessity of making the eligibility requirements for natural mothers and adoptive parents more equitable.

June 2, 1983
Unemployment Insurance Act
We on this side of the House have seen this need for many years and I myself have dealt with many cases where this inequity has arisen. Having a family is a shared responsibility of both mother and father. If we are to encourage planned parenthood, then the Government must also share in the responsibility, assuring women that they will be treated equally and be equally protected by our safety nets.
The changes which are proposed to the Unemployment Insurance Act would simplify what has fast become an administrative nightmare with respect to collecting maternity benefits. I ask Your Honour if you have ever tried to explain to an expectant mother why she cannot collect maternity benefits when she meets the requirements for a major attachment to the work-force, having the necessary 20 insured weeks, but does not have the "magic ten" to qualify. It is almost impossible to make sense out of this particular section of the legislation.
What is meant by the "magic ten" is that a woman must have conceived between the thirtieth and fiftieth week prior to the expected date of her confinement. In other words, she is required to have worked for at least ten weeks around the time of conception. This requirement, I feel, is absolutely ludicrous. A woman may have had a long working history and been a major and consistent member of the labour force. Because of circumstances beyond her control, she may have been out of the labour force for more than the ten weeks during this unique period between the thirtieth and fiftieth week prior to her confinement. Consequently, she would not qualify for maternity benefits. There are hundreds of women who have had well over the required 20 weeks which would give qualification for sick benefits but who are missing the "magic ten" and therefore do not qualify for maternity benefits.
An even more blatant example of discrimination against women is that of the present denial of benefits to adoptive mothers. In all cases where an adoption is planned, the parents must provide proof to the adoption agency that they are financially secure and can provide an adequate, secure home for the new child. Women in this category, who have had a longstanding and major attachment to the work-force and who suffer an interruption of earnings in order to be home with the new baby, as is required by adoptive authorities, especially here in Ontario where it is a requirement that one must be at home for a period of six months, cannot collect unemployment insurance benefits during this interruption.
In the majority of cases of adopting parents, the mother has been working for a number of years while trying to conceive a child. When the decision to adopt is made, she will have been well established in the work force. However, under present regulations, she will have to give up the seniority of all those years of work. In effect, she is being punished because she cannot have children naturally and therefore cannot collect maternity benefits. She is not only denied the experience of bearing a child for various reasons but is also being denied the income protection that is afforded to natural mothers.
As I said at the outset, the program was initially set up to provide income protection for workers suffering temporary income interruptions. I have outlined examples of blatant discrimination in its application toward women with respect to their contributions to the labour force, to the family unit and to society. As legislation was introduced and passed to pay benefits to those members of the labour force who have suffered temporary interruptions of earnings, those benefits must be made available to both men and women in a fair and equitable manner without discrimination.
Today we are debating the adoption of legislation and amendments to the Act that will provide a more fair and equitable payment to all concerned. I thank you for the opportunity to debate today, Mr. Speaker.

That is quite clearly within the legislation. This is not a deviation from that principle. That principle is part of the principle of this legislation. What we are doing is saying in essence that the same principle be extended whether adopted or natural parents are involved. I would argue that there is no deviation from what we now have before us.
I admit it is a broadening of one section, but it is a broadening consistent with what is already contained within the legislation that applies to other citizens of Canada. I suggest it is wrong to give to one what you are not prepared to give to others.
On the second point, the matter of whether it entails additional expenditure, it quite clearly does not. The expenditure that we are speaking about is the exact same expenditure, but to be shared with either of the parents. We are saying that the amount of money talked about is no more and no less than the amount of money currently put forward under the Royal
Proclamation, and that either of the parents should have access to the allowance.
The amount that we are talking about, both in terms of the amount of time that is to be made available and the amount of money, is quite clearly the same, involving the same expenditure. Therefore there has been no attempt made by us to increase the expenditures. In fact, Mr. Chairman, I might point out to you that it is entirely possible that we are speaking about a smaller amount of money. In fact, we could be speaking about less money than the Minister is currently putting forward.
I put to you, Sir, that in the case of a family where the wife earns $20,000 a year and the husband earns less, if the husband were to decide to be the parent in receipt of benefit, then he would receive benefit at a lesser amount since his entitlement would be a lesser entitlement.
I would therefore argue that we are not in any way trying to increase the expenditure of the Government. We are simply trying to make it possible for the family unit, something that all of us in the House support and that all of us think is so important for the future of the country, to make the decision for itself as to which of the two parents should stay home during that period immediately after the birth of the child. When that choice has been made by that family, the Unemployment Insurance Act should then recognize that right of choice, and having made that recognition the payment should be made to either of the parents, which ever one is designated to be the recipient.

I think it would be unfortunate if we were to pass this moment in Committee without paying that tribute to Stella Bliss and all the Stella Blisses of the world.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I now want to put a question to the Minister, without diminishing in any way our support for this amendment. My question is prompted by our concern for the state of the Unemployment Insurance Fund. Based on the experience of the past five months, the expenditure will exceed $12 billion this year. Last year it reached a record high of $8 billion. I put the question to the Hon. Minister now that I put to him in committee the other day when we were dealing with his Estimates. Can the Minister give the Committee an assurance that there will not be an increase in Unemployment Insurance premiums? In my view and in the view of my colleagues, an increase in Unemployment Insurance premiums would impose a disincentive on the private sector, expecially small business firms, to hire people because it would impose an additional tax upon them. It would also impose an additional hardship upon women who are the lower paid members of our society and who would have to pay additional Unemployment Insurance premiums.
Unemployment Insurance Act
Can the Minister first give us some idea of how much the amendments will cost in terms of additional benefits, and can he then tell us how he intends to finance them? If at the same time, he can give us an assurance that he does not anticipate an increase in the premiums, we would be very satisfied.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, what I can offer to the Hon. Member is the very clear commitment that we intend to maintain insurance premiums at the lowest possible level. I cannot assure him that premiums will not increase because it is not wholly my assurance to give.
I would like to explain to Members of the Committee that before we arrive at decisions about premium increases, we first undertake an examination of what the various rates both of employment and unemployment are projected to be for the third quarter of the fiscal year, what the draw on the fund has been, and what we might see as the projected deficit in 1984. On the basis of those soundings and, as was done last year, on the basis of the kind of consultations I would undertake through the Commission with business and labour, we would then make recommendations to the Minister of Finance and to Cabinet who would then have to make the final decision.
I can, however, make it very clear that it is my belief that we will not have to raise premiums substantially in the forthcoming year unless the Hon. Member for St. John's East falls into the trap that is being laid by the recommendations of some of his colleagues. In particular, I read in the paper this morning that the Hon. Member from Etobicoke is recommending a totally uncapped extension of Unemployment Insurance benefits, a move that would probably add $4 billion or $5 billion to the cost of unemployment insurance. Substantially higher premiums would be required to begin to pay for that. If the Hon. Member for St. John's East will guarantee me that he will not endorse the position taken by his colleague, the Hon. Member from Etobicoke, I will assure him that I will do my best to make sure premiums stay at a very low level.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND

The Minister knows full well, but deliberately omitted to say, that when a person no longer receives Unemployment Insurance benefits, when he becomes an exhaustee, he still has to live, and in order to live he must subject himself to a means test to qualify for welfare.
The Minister also knows that the Government of Canada pays 50 per cent of the welfare bill under the Canada Assistance Plan. This proposal would certainly save money under the Canada Assistance Plan, it would save the money of the hard-pressed Provinces. A case could be made, albeit in another forum because this is not the day for it, to think in terms of changing the whole approach to unemployment insur-

ance to fit into the reality of the period that we are going through at the present time.
This proposal speaks to displacement as a result of high tech, the impact that it will have on women, the impact it is having on young people and how the Unemployment Insurance Act can relate to this new situation. I cannot give any assurance to the Minister, but I have every right to ask the Minister if he intends to raise premiums. I have every right to ask the Minister what in his opinion are the estimated additional charges on the Unemployment Insurance Fund that will flow from the passage of these amendments. subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, far from being facetious, I was being very serious, pointing out that we take quite seriously the state of the Unemployment Insurance Fund. That is why we have given very serious consideration in the past to finding the best way of coping with those who have exhausted their benefits.
I want to point out to the Committee that while we recognize that hardships are faced by those who exhaust their benefits, a study conducted last Fall showed that on average about 6 or 8 per cent of those end up on welfare. The figures could be substantially higher-perhaps as high as 12 per cent or 13 per cent. Not everyone who exhausts benefits immediately goes on welfare. About 40 per cent go back to work within five or six weeks and some others go back to school or find some other means of support. Only a small proportion make application for welfare.
We feel that we have made a substantial offer to alleviate that problem under the NEED program which was started with $500 million. Because of the leverage we have established with the private sector and the Provinces, it will be closer to $900 million by the time we are finished. We have been able to provide well over 60,000 jobs which should be properly cha-nelled for those who otherwise have to make a choice. That is a way of cushioning it.
The alternative, and this is very important to the Hon. Member for St. John's East and others who have made the case, is having an open-ended commitment, and even if we had a limited 26-week extension that would place an additional cost on the Unemployment Insurance Fund of anywhere from $3 billion to $4 billion. That would have to be raised either through premiums or further Government deficit financing. We have heard many comments from the other side of the House to the effect that we should not go into further deficit financing. That is the dilemma we face and that is why it is important that we not fall into the trap of saying we should automatically extend benefits. That would be a very costly charge against the fund and the money would have to be raised either by Government borrowing or higher premiums.
I agree with the Hon. Member that the Unemployment Insurance Act must change if it is to be relevant. That is why I
have suggested that we use the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration as a forum in which Members can make representations and where people can examine the Unemployment Insurance Act. Then when we come back to the House next time for amendments to the Act we will have had the full benefit of their representations.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND

Mr. Speaker, I would like to have taken advantage of the debate on the amendment to discuss a question that might just as well have been placed under clause 3 if we were going to move ahead, but I see the clock is running out and we are about to go down the chute, as far as any further discussion is concerned. I think this is an important place to put the question of improvements to the legislation, especially if there is no objection to them in the House, which I think is illustrated by the consent that was given on the amendment.
I should like to make two comments in relation to administration of the legislation. The provisions of this Bill are obviously going to cause some further work load for the Unemployment Insurance Commission staff. The administrative burden of the Unemployment Insurance Commission offices in the regions which 1 represent and in others, has reached the point that they often cannot deliver service. Because of the complexity of the task, the lack of staff and training, some claimants are as much as 12 weeks behind in receiving their benefits. They are left without income for that time. Last winter the welfare system, acting on an emergency basis, was unable to provide support for them.
When the Minister says there are no additional costs that will go into the system, I wonder if he is fulfilling his responsibility to provide sufficient staff and sufficient resources and sufficient training to ensure that the additional burden and the more complicated approach to providing unemployment insurance is being dealt with in an appropriate way.
An example is the case of a great many claims of loggers and fishermen coming in at a certain time of the year as shut-downs occur. The Minister's training staff does not train unemployment insurance officers on a regular basis to evaluate those claims, which are very complex so there is a tremendous shortage of personnel who can handle these claims. This causes enormous delays.
Could the Minister give us an indication of what his Department is doing to ensure that people will not have to wait up to 12 weeks for benefits because of the more complicated provisions of the Act. What is he doing about special agents with the responsibility of dealing with large numbers of groups so that they can be moved through quickly?
The second matter I want to raise also relates to administration, and that is the access that individuals-women, adoptive parents or any other group-have to their files. Individuals in the community are being systematically denied access to their unemployment insurance files when they have questions about their entitlement or the decisions made by unemployment insurance officials. (1.2)	Notwithstanding anything in this Act, self-employed fishermen and persons engaged in any activity related to or incidental to fishing shall qualify for unemployment insurance, including, as an employer of a self-employed person engaged in fishing, any person with whom the self-employed person enters into a contractual or other commercial relationship in respect of his occupation as a self-employed person engaged in fishing.
